package_info.package_manager: Custom/Unknown (malware targeting ICS/SCADA devices, not distributed via public package managers)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (modular malware suite, not versioned in the traditional sense)
package_info.why_malicious: The malware suite is specifically designed to compromise, disrupt, and manipulate industrial control systems (ICS) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) devices. It enables attackers to enumerate, control, and sabotage critical infrastructure by exploiting device protocols, brute-forcing credentials, and leveraging known vulnerabilities in engineering workstations. The tools provide full system access, lateral movement, and device manipulation capabilities, representing a severe threat to operational technology environments.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when executed on engineering workstation or within ICS network)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode representing TAGRUN OPC UA scanner behavior
connect_to_opc_ua_server(target_ip)
enumerate_tags_and_structure()
brute_force_credentials()
read_tag_values()
write_tag_values()
malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or Python)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code connects to OPC UA servers, enumerates their structure and tags, brute-forces credentials, and reads/writes tag values, enabling unauthorized access and manipulation of industrial processes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Enumerating tags, brute-forcing credentials, and reading/writing tag values on OPC UA servers is highly indicative of reconnaissance and manipulation activity, not normal engineering operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate engineering tools do not brute-force credentials or indiscriminately enumerate and manipulate all tags on a production system.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Engineering tools may enumerate tags and read/write values during commissioning or troubleshooting, but not via brute-force or without authentication.
key_indicators: Bulk enumeration of OPC UA tags

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode representing CODECALL Modbus attack behavior
connect_to_modicon_plc(target_ip)
scan_device()
read_plc_memory()
write_plc_memory()
issue_control_commands()
malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or Python)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code connects to Schneider Electric Modicon PLCs using the Modbus protocol, scans devices, reads and writes PLC memory, and issues control commands, enabling device manipulation and potential sabotage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly reading and writing PLC memory and issuing control commands outside of authorized engineering sessions is highly suspicious and can disrupt or damage industrial processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal engineering software does not perform unauthorized memory manipulation or control command execution on PLCs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use may occur during device commissioning or maintenance, but only by authorized personnel with proper authentication.

malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or Python)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code connects to Omron PLCs and servo drives, scans devices, reads and writes servo drive parameters, enabling manipulation of industrial machinery operation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unauthorized access and manipulation of servo drive parameters can cause physical damage or unsafe operation of industrial equipment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal operations do not involve unscheduled or unauthorized parameter changes on servo drives.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate engineering tasks may involve parameter changes, but only under strict controls and authentication.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when executed on Windows engineering workstation)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode representing ASRock driver exploit
load_vulnerable_asrock_driver()
exploit_driver_to_escalate_privileges()
gain_system_access()
malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or PowerShell)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads a vulnerable ASRock motherboard driver and exploits it to escalate privileges on the Windows engineering workstation, enabling full system compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exploiting known vulnerable drivers for privilege escalation is a common malware technique and is not part of normal engineering workstation operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not load or exploit vulnerable drivers to gain elevated privileges.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; privilege escalation via driver exploit is always malicious.
key_indicators: Loading of known vulnerable ASRock driver

attack_chain.action: Initial compromise of engineering workstation, possibly via phishing or supply chain attack.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malware components on the workstation

attack_chain.action: Privilege escalation on engineering workstation using ASRock driver exploit.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system access and ability to deploy ICS attack modules

attack_chain.action: Network reconnaissance and enumeration of ICS/SCADA devices (OPC UA servers, PLCs).
Brute-force credentials and gain unauthorized access to ICS devices.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to read/write tag values and manipulate device state

attack_chain.action: Manipulation of PLC memory, tag values, and servo drive parameters to disrupt or sabotage industrial processes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disruption, degradation, or damage to ICS/SCADA operations (final goal)

behavioral_signatures: Bulk enumeration of OPC UA tags and structure
Brute-force authentication attempts against OPC UA servers
Unauthorized Modbus protocol activity targeting PLCs
Unscheduled or unauthorized read/write operations on PLC memory or servo drive parameters
Loading and exploitation of known vulnerable ASRock motherboard drivers
file_indicators: Presence of unknown binaries on engineering workstations
Unexpected driver files related to ASRock hardware
Malware components named TAGRUN, CODECALL, OMSHELL, EVILSCHOLAR, BADOMEN, DUSTTUNNEL, MOUSEHOLE, LAZYCARGO
network_indicators: Unusual OPC UA and Modbus network traffic from engineering workstations
Connections to PLCs and OPC UA servers outside of scheduled maintenance windows
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor engineering workstations and OT networks for unauthorized enumeration of OPC UA tags, brute-force authentication attempts, and unscheduled Modbus/Omron protocol activity. Detect loading of vulnerable ASRock drivers and privilege escalation attempts. Flag any binaries or processes matching known malware component names or exhibiting these behaviors. Correlate network activity with scheduled maintenance to identify suspicious access patterns.
